articles.title: Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work, but with Apple's first touchscreen MacBook now here, John Ternus says you've gotta touch it to believe it
articles.summary: For 16 years, Apple had an answer ready whenever someone asked about a touchscreen Mac, and the answer was always some version of no.
articles.body: For 16 years, Apple had an answer ready whenever someone asked about a touchscreen Mac, and the answer was always some version of no.Steve Jobs gave it first, with the most theatre. Tim Cook gave it with kitchen appliances, and Phil Schiller with user studies. In 2021, Apple's then hardware engineering chief, John Ternus, told The Wall Street Journal's Joanna Stern that the Mac was built around the keyboard and trackpad, adding: "We haven't really felt a reason to change that."Apple has now found one.The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a mouthful even by Apple's standards, so I'll call it the touchscreen MacBook Pro from here on. It is the first Mac that responds to a finger on its screen, and also the first MacBook with an OLED panel, which, as Apple tells it, is the very reason touch could happen at all.When Wired asked Ternus, now nearly two months into the CEO job, whether Apple was about to break its oldest Mac taboo, he kept it brief: "Who knew?" On X, he was a little less brief, writing that Apple was "glowing with excitement" over the new MacBook Pro and that "you've gotta touch it to believe it." With the glowing Apple logo back on the lid, the pun was almost certainly intended.That is quite a turn for someone who, five years ago, couldn't see a reason to change the Mac at all, and Apple can expect some ribbing for it. The reversal is also typical of how the company works. Apple's "never" has usually carried an unwritten condition, roughly "until we can do it in a way we like," and no product has taken longer to get past it than the touchscreen Mac.Apple kept saying no, and nobody else quite proved it wrongJobs set the tone in October 2010, barely ten months after he had introduced the iPad. Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical, he argued on stage. Reaching up to a laptop screen made for a nice demo, but Apple's own testing showed fatigue set in quickly, and after long enough, "your arm wants to fall off." Touch belonged on horizontal surfaces, which is why MacBooks got big glass trackpads instead.Cook made a similar case two years later. Asked on a 2012 earnings call whether tablets and laptops would eventually merge, he likened the idea to combining "a toaster and a refrigerator," suggesting the result would please nobody. Microsoft released its first Surface tablets that same year, alongside a version of Windows rebuilt around touch.Then came Schiller. In 2015, Apple's marketing chief laid out a broader theory of the product line to journalist Steven Levy: every Apple device is essentially a computer behind a sheet of glass, and each gets the interface that suits how it is used. Reaching over a fixed keyboard to poke a screen was uncomfortable, he argued, and macOS was built for the precision of a pointer, with tiny buttons and dense menus that fingers would fumble.A year later, Apple did put touch on the MacBook Pro, just not on the display. The Touch Bar sat above the keyboard, and Schiller said the company had tested touchscreen Macs internally and come away convinced its instincts were right. The Touch Bar itself didn't last. Physical function keys returned in 2021, and the strip was gone from the lineup by 2023.Stern, for her part, kept asking. When she put the question to software chief Craig Federighi at the Journal's Tech Live event in October 2022, he replied "Who's to say?" and the panel broke into laughter. By June 2025, Federighi and marketing head Greg Joswiak were meeting it with laughter alone. Going back through her archive on X this week, Stern noted that Apple's replies had slowly drifted from a flat "nope" to evasive laughter.In hindsight, that was about as close to a yes as Apple ever gets.Elsewhere, in the Windows world, touchscreen laptops became routine long ago. Machines with screens you can tap, and often fold back into a tablet, have sat on store shelves for well over a decade without ever being short of buyers. A generation raised on phones and tablets expects every screen to respond to touch, and plenty of laptops happily oblige.Selling them, though, isn't the same as settling the argument, and Microsoft's own history shows it. Windows 8 rebuilt the PC around touch, and the backlash was strong enough that the Start button came back within a year. Windows 10 restored the familiar desktop, Windows 11 quietly dropped the dedicated tablet mode, and the company that bet hardest on touchscreen laptops has spent the decade since easing touch into the background. Part of the reason is that the trade-offs never went away. A touchscreen still tends to mean a glossier panel, more weight and shorter battery life, and with most apps never rethought for fingers, people were rarely given a good reason to reach for the screen.Apple, meanwhile, was edging closer from the other side. The iPad picked up trackpad support in 2020 and a far more Mac-like iPadOS last year, complete with resizable windows and a menu bar. The Mac, in turn, had been running iPhone and iPad apps since its move to Apple silicon, apps built for fingers that never felt quite right under a cursor.By January 2023, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman was reporting that Apple had a touchscreen MacBook Pro in the works, originally pencilled in for 2025. That date slipped, and for good reason. Apple had clearly decided a touchscreen Mac was coming; what it hadn't worked out yet was how to add one without giving anything up.Touch could only come if it cost the Mac nothingTernus's explanation for the timing is the most revealing part of this story. Apple, he told Wired, needed to reach a point where adding touch didn't make the MacBook Pro worse in any way: not heavier, not thicker. Anything earlier would have meant a compromise on the company's most expensive laptop.The OLED panel is what made the maths work. The touch sensor is built directly into the display rather than laid on top as a separate layer, so it adds neither bulk nor noticeable lag, and because OLED needs no backlight, the lid slims down too. The 16-inch model now weighs about 1.8kg, roughly 300 grams less than before, while the 14-inch drops to around 1.36kg. Both are marginally thinner, and slimmer borders stretch the screens to 14.2 and 16.3 inches.Apple calls it the best laptop display in the world, and the numbers support the claim. The tandem OLED panel stacks two light-emitting layers to hit 2,000 nits in both HDR and everyday SDR use, with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, a refresh rate that moves between 10Hz and 120Hz, and colour that spans both P3 and Adobe RGB.For photographers, and I count myself among them, that last detail will matter more than any tap or swipe.The smaller decisions tell you how seriously Apple took the ergonomics argument it once made against itself. The hinge has been redesigned to keep the display steady under a finger, though early demo footage still shows a slight bounce on a firm tap. The cooling system now pushes warm air away from the panel so it doesn't feel hot to the touch. Even the webcam has been considered, with stabilisation that smooths the video feed when you tap the screen mid-call.Software is where Schiller's old objections have been dealt with most directly. macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn't throw out the desktop the way Windows 8 did with its tiles. The menu bar and windows look as they always have, but in the demos Wired saw, menu items and the little traffic-light buttons grew as a finger reached them, so a tap lands where it should. Looking back, the rounder buttons and roomier menu bar that came with Liquid Glass were clearly groundwork.Apps that haven't been updated still respond, because macOS simply translates a tap into a click, and the Dynamic Island crosses over from the iPhone as the new home for Spotlight, Live Activities and Siri AI. Apple's own apps go further, with a multi-touch keyboard in Logic Pro and pinch-to-zoom on a cut in Final Cut Pro, while apps from Lightroom and DaVinci Resolve to Blender and Microsoft Office are lining up support.Apple's footnote is less eager. Those apps arrive later this year, and as with the iPhone Duo, where many apps are still being updated for the folding screen, it may be a while before touch feels at home across the Mac.Jobs would still mind the tired arms, and Apple knows itThe pricing makes the intended audience clear. The 14-inch model with M5 Pro starts at Rs 3,49,900 in India and the 16-inch at Rs 4,09,900, while the M5 Max versions begin at Rs 5,49,900 and Rs 5,89,900. In the US, the two start at $2,899 and $3,399, and a fully specced 16-inch model climbs all the way to $14,549.Joswiak's case, as he put it to Wired, is that Apple's professional users already own an iPad and an iPhone, and that a younger generation of creators simply expects a screen to respond to touch. The MacBook Air and iMac don't get it, and Ternus, predictably, wouldn't say whether they ever will. Apple has made a neat case for what touch can do for colourists, musicians and developers, but the harder sell will come if it ever reaches the MacBook Air, where Apple will face the same question Windows laptops never quite answered for everyday buyers: why anyone needs to reach for the screen at all.Nobody is being pushed into it, either. The regular 14-inch MacBook Pro, refreshed only a day earlier with Apple's newer M6 chip, stays on the shelves without a touchscreen. That leaves buyers with a slightly odd choice: the touchscreen model gets the better display, while the one without it gets the newer processor.Which brings us to Jobs.It's easy to picture him furious, and plenty of longtime Apple fans will insist this would never have happened on his watch. I'm not so sure.Jobs said a lot of things on stage that Apple later quietly undid. He maintained the company had no interest in making a phone, right up until the iPhone. He waved off video on the iPod until the hardware could handle it. In 2007, he said that if you see a stylus, "they blew it," and Apple now sells a Pencil that works with the iPad and the new iPhone Duo. In almost every case, his no was aimed at the version of an idea that existed at the time.The touchscreen laptop of 2010 fits that pattern. It was usually a touch layer added to an ordinary laptop screen, running software built for a mouse, and his complaint about holding an arm up to it was fair. Sixteen years on, nobody has offered a convincing answer to it, and Apple isn't trying to: the trackpad hasn't shrunk, and Ternus still describes the Mac as an indirect input device first. Touch here is for the moments when reaching out is quicker than steering a cursor, whether that's nudging a colour wheel, playing a chord, pinching into a photo or tapping a Live Activity.So what would Jobs say? He would probably still tell you your arm will get tired, and he would be right. Then he would likely ask whether the screen underneath was the best Apple had ever made, whether touch had cost the machine a single gram or millimetre, and whether macOS still felt like macOS.This MacBook Pro has an answer to each of those, and getting there took 16 years. For a company whose co-founder once called touchscreen laptops "ergonomically terrible," taking that long to say yes might be the most Jobs-like thing it has done in a while.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Did you put pumpkin in the khichdi?’: Richa Chadha reveals how Ali Fazal’s hands-on parenting sometimes turns into micromanaging, even from another city
articles.summary: Sometimes, parenting conversations at home are not about bedtime routines or screen time. They are about what went into the khichdi.
articles.body: Sometimes, parenting conversations at home are not about bedtime routines or screen time. They are about what went into the khichdi. For actors Richa Chadha and Ali Fazal, even a simple meal for their daughter can become a topic of discussion, especially when one parent wants to know every little detail.Speaking to Moviefied, Richa offered a glimpse into Ali’s approach to fatherhood, describing him as deeply involved in caring for their daughter, Zuneyra Ida Fazal. While she appreciates his attention and affection, she admitted that his enthusiasm can occasionally feel like micromanagement. Her example was simple but telling. Even while Ali was away in Srinagar, he wanted to know whether she had added pumpkin to their daughter’s khichdi. It was the kind of question that could come from concern, but also one that left Richa feeling that he might be checking a little too closely.A father who wants to know every detailRicha’s account suggests that Ali likes to stay connected to his daughter’s daily routine, even when work takes him away from home. She described him as someone who is “obsessed with his daughter”, adding that his involvement can sometimes become a little much. The pumpkin question captured this perfectly. Ali was not at home, yet he was checking on a small detail of his daughter’s meal. For a parent who wants to remain involved from a distance, such questions may feel like a way of participating in everyday care. For the parent managing things at home, however, repeated checks can feel unnecessary.Richa also pointed out that they have a nanny at home and that she is actively involved in looking after their daughter. Despite this support, Ali remains particular about how things are being handled. “He is a little extra,” she said, describing the side of his parenting that can sometimes irritate her. Her comments were light-hearted, but they offered a relatable picture of how couples can have different ideas about what being involved in childcare should look like.When care starts feeling like micromanagementAli’s habit raises a familiar question for many parents: where does involvement end and micromanagement begin? Being attentive to a child’s food, sleep, health and routine is a normal part of parenting. Parents often ask questions because they want to ensure their child is safe and cared for. When they are away from home, checking in may also help them feel connected to what is happening. But when every small decision becomes a matter for discussion, the other parent may feel that their judgement is being questioned. Even well-intentioned questions can become tiring if they arrive too frequently or leave little room for the person at home to make decisions independently.That does not automatically mean the parent asking questions is distrustful. It may simply reflect different approaches to responsibility, a desire to remain involved or uncertainty about how to share childcare when one parent is away. Richa’s comments do not suggest that Ali’s concern comes from a lack of trust. Instead, her anecdote shows how affection and over-involvement can sometimes exist side by side. The challenge for parents is to communicate their expectations and find a balance that allows both to contribute without feeling monitored.How Richa and Ali are finding their parenting rhythmRicha and Ali married in 2022 and welcomed their daughter in July 2024. Since becoming parents, they have had to make room for family responsibilities alongside demanding acting careers. Their circumstances mean that childcare involves planning, coordination and adjustments to work schedules. In previous public conversations, the couple have discussed managing professional commitments while ensuring that one of them can be available for their daughter.Richa has also spoken about taking time to recover after childbirth and wanting privacy during the early period of motherhood. These experiences reflect how becoming parents can change everyday priorities, from professional decisions to the way household responsibilities are shared. Every family develops its own rhythm. Some couples divide tasks according to their schedules, while others stay involved in decisions together. Problems can arise when one person feels responsible for carrying out the daily work but also has to answer repeated questions about how it is being done. In such situations, clear communication can help. Agreeing on important matters, such as a child’s health and dietary needs, while allowing flexibility in everyday choices can make shared parenting easier.Beneath the pumpkin question is a lot of loveFor all the humour in Richa’s story, the image of Ali checking on his daughter’s khichdi from Srinagar is also a glimpse into how seriously he takes fatherhood. He wants to know what she is eating and how she is being cared for, even when he cannot be physically present. At the same time, Richa’s reaction highlights another side of parenting: being a hands-on parent also means recognising when to trust the other person to handle things.Their exchange is not a lesson in perfect parenting. It is a small, everyday moment between two people learning how to raise a child together while managing work, distance and different expectations. Ali may want a detailed update about the pumpkin. Richa may sometimes wish he would leave the khichdi questions alone. Both reactions can exist in a family where parents are trying to do their best. And perhaps that is what makes the anecdote so relatable. Sometimes, modern parenting is not about having all the answers. It is about learning when to check in, when to step back and when to trust that the person at home has everything under control.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ARDF plans to expand research beyond areca
articles.summary: ARDF to amend trust deed to expand research beyond arecanut to black pepper, coffee, cocoa and rubber; plans summit, govt recognition, labs and university ties.
articles.body: Mangaluru: The Arecanut Research and Development Foundation (ARDF) has decided to amend its trust deed to expand its research activities beyond arecanut to include black pepper, coffee, cocoa and rubber.The decision was taken at a meeting of the ARDF held under the chairmanship of Dharmasthala Dharmadhikari D Veerendra Heggade, recently. During the meeting, ARDF managing trustee and Campco president SR Satishchandra said 34 arecanut samples had been received by the foundation from the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) and the customs department for examination during the current year. He said the development reflected the recognition ARDF has been receiving at the national level.The meeting also discussed plans to organise an International Arecanut Summit next year in collaboration with Campco. Heggade assured his full cooperation for the proposed summit.The members held detailed discussions on securing govt-level recognition for ARDF. It was decided to explore collaborations with universities and govt departments involved in agricultural research. The foundation also plans to enter into suitable agreements for establishing well-equipped laboratories and a library, besides appointing the staff required to support its research activities.The meeting decided to obtain the necessary details from Mangalore University and initiate further action.Campco MD and ARDF trustee BV Satyanarayana; ARDF executive officer Keshava Bhat; Areca Mahamandala vice-president Suryanarayana; MAMCOS, Shivamogga, vice-president Mahesh HS; TSS director Narasimha Hegde; TUMCOS, Channagiri, managing director Madhu and special invitee Vigneshwara Varmudy were present.Stay updated with the latest Mangaluru news. articles.title: Bangladesh regime change: Hasina's ouster was planned days before Aug 5, says Yusuf's aide
articles.summary: A journalist working for French news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP) acted as an intermediary between student leaders in Bangladesh and Nobel laureate
articles.body: A journalist working for French news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP) acted as an intermediary between student leaders in Bangladesh and Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus before Sheikh Hasina was forced from power in August 2024, according to a claim by Yunus's former press secretary Shafiqul Alam.In a Facebook post on October 28, Alam alleged that Qadaruddin Shishir, who was then with AFP's fact-checking team in Dhaka, helped arrange initial discussions between Yunus and student leaders who wanted him to head an interim government after Hasina's departure.Alam's account suggests that discussions about who would lead Bangladesh after Hasina had begun before she fled the country on August 5, 2024.Describing how the contact was established, Alam wrote: "When student leaders wanted to reach out to Nobel Laureate Professor Muhammad Yunus and invite him to head the interim government in a post-Hasina scenario, they needed a trusted bridge-builder. Qadaruddin Shishir stepped up to fulfill that critical role."Alam said Shishir managed the discussions discreetly while working alongside him at the AFP bureau in Dhaka."At the time, Shishir was the editor of AFP Dhaka Fact Check team. Sitting just a yard away from my desk in the AFP Dhaka bureau, he managed this high-stakes operation in complete secrecy. Only a select few trusted individuals knew what was happening. It was Shishir who first approached the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize winner on behalf of the student leaders and facilitated the initial talks between the two parties."According to Alam, the initial contact took place two days before Hasina's departure. He claimed the secrecy was essential because the then prime minister's security apparatus could have discovered the discussions."Hasina would remain in power for two more days, yet her brutal security machine—notorious for mass killings and abductions—never caught a whisper of it. Had they discovered what was happening, Shishir and our entire AFP team would likely have ended up in an Aynaghar (house of mirrors secret prison)."Aynaghar is the name associated with a secret detention facility in Bangladesh, where allegations of enforced disappearances and torture have been reported.Alam also said Shishir had been collecting video evidence of violence during the crackdown on protesters."Throughout it all, Shishir remained remarkably cool and composed, even as he quietly started gathering video evidence of the cold-blooded murders being committed by the regime."Yunus took charge after Hasina fledThe student-led protests began in July 2024 as an agitation against government job quotas before escalating into a wider movement against Hasina's government. She fled Bangladesh on August 5 amid the unrest.On August 6, student protest leaders publicly proposed Yunus as the head of an interim administration. He returned to Dhaka from Paris and took office as chief adviser on August 8.The revelations in Alam's post add details about the contacts that preceded Yunus's appointment. They also raise questions about how student leaders prepared for a possible transition of power before Hasina's departure.However, evidence of discussions about a successor does not, by itself, prove that the protests as a whole were planned or controlled by a single group. Alam's account has not independently established the extent of coordination between the student leadership and other actors.Hasina has since accused the Yunus administration of political persecution and failing to hold those responsible for violence accountable. Yunus's interim administration governed Bangladesh until February 2026, when it handed over power following the election of Tarique Rahman as prime minister.You use AI every day.
